papers.title: Somnus, a tunable, open-source platform for automated EEG sleep scoring in physiological and disease mouse models.
papers.abstract: Many studies using mouse models of human brain disorders rely on extended recordings of brain electrical activity through electroencephalogram, or EEG. The features that researchers measure in these recordings, such as seizures and epileptiform activity, are deeply influenced by whether the animal is awake, in non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, or in rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. Because total sleep duration varies naturally across animals, rigorous experimental comparisons require classifying the sleep state of every few seconds of a recording. Manual annotation is highly labor-intensive, often requiring hours per subject. While automated scoring tools accelerate this process, they are typically trained exclusively on healthy cohorts and frequently fail when applied to disease models that exhibit atypical or fragmented sleep architecture. Somnus is an open-source Python package designed to automate rodent sleep staging using EEG, muscle activity (EMG), and optional video-tracking data. It includes a robust base model trained on diverse recordings from six independent laboratories, enabling out-of-the-box classification across various equipment setups without requiring prior manual labeling. A central feature of Somnus is its capacity for rapid adaptation to pathological sleep structure. The software provides a graphical interface that directs researchers to the specific epochs where the base model is least certain. Users can manually correct these targeted epochs in a built-in viewer by comparing the model's classification to the raw EEG signal and video, and then use their corrections to fine-tune the model. This workflow empowers researchers to generate accurate custom scorers for complex disease models or novel treatments with just a few minutes of manual correction, bypassing the need to hand-score entire experimental cohorts or develop their own models from scratch.

papers.title: Isoflurane anesthesia CNS recovery state: ultra-slow oscillations and cellular-stress-responsive gene expression.
papers.abstract: General anesthesia and NREM sleep share slow-wave EEG features, yet whether anesthesia substitutes for physiological sleep remains unclear. We compared recovery from 4h of isoflurane anesthesia (IA) with time-matched sleep and sleep deprivation (SD) in male C57BL/6J mice using continuous EEG/EMG recordings and frontal cortex RNA sequencing. IA recovery produced transient, rebound arousal, reduced early NREM and REM sleep, and, fragmented subsequent NREM bouts, and persistant, ultra-slow EEG-oscillations that normalized within two weeks. Whereas, SD induced consolidated rebound sleep and slow wave activity. Transcriptomic profiling at ZT6 showed that IA and SD induced largely distinct cortical gene-expression programs. IA preferentially enriched integrated stress response and unfolded protein response genes, whereas SD showed a comparatively orthogonal, growth-permissive, mTOR-associated profile. Although IA-induced gene-expression suggests cellular stress, corticosterone measurements argued against systemic stress as the primary driver. These findings indicate that isoflurane recovery is neurophysiologically and molecularly distinct from restorative sleep.

papers.title: Interfloor noise triggers sleep fragmentation and affective deficits via dysregulation of the orexin-serotonin axis and hippocampal synaptic plasticity.
papers.abstract: Residential interfloor noise is an urban stressor with unknown neurobiological effects on sleep and mood. This study aimed to elucidate the effects of interfloor noise on sleep architecture, affective behavior, and molecular biomarkers using a mouse model. The post-exposure sleep-wake states of male C57BL/6 mice exposed to simulated interfloor noise (70-100 dB) for 12 h daily for 7 days were monitored via piezoelectric sensing, which was followed by behavioral tests for anxiety- and depression-like phenotypes. Molecular analyses were performed to quantify neuroendocrine, neuroinflammatory, neurotransmitter, and synaptic plasticity markers in the hypothalamus and hippocampus. Exploratory hippocampal RNA-seq was used to assess transcriptomic alterations. Seven days of interfloor noise exposure induced sleep fragmentation (increased bout frequency and shortened duration) and selectively reduced REM sleep while preserving total and NREM sleep. Mice exposed to interfloor noise exhibited anxiety-like behaviors and behavioral despair, and molecularly, they had increased hypothalamic cytokines (tumor necrosis factor-α, interleukin-6, and interleukin-1β) and decreased serum corticosterone. Interfloor noise induced hypothalamic orexin-serotonin dysregulation, increased hippocampal GABAergic signaling, and reduced hippocampal HTR1A, HTR2A, BDNF, PSD95, and p-ERK expression. Hypothalamic markers were correlated with sleep disruption, whereas hippocampal markers were correlated with anxiety. RNA-seq revealed the upregulation of Hif3a and oxygen response transcriptomic changes, indicating an additional hippocampal stress response. The 7-day interfloor noise paradigm provides a valid mouse model for REM sleep disruption, fragmentation, and mood deficits. This study offers a platform for future mechanistic and interventional studies of interfloor noise-induced disorders.

The paradigm is proposed as a mouse model for noise-induced REM sleep disruption and mood deficits.

papers.title: From labels to latents: revealing state-dependent hippocampal computations and non-spatial replay with Jump Latent Variable Model.
papers.abstract: Neural activity is often interpreted by imposing external labels (e.g., position during locomotion) and decoding within that space (e.g. replay). While powerful, such supervision can mask structure in the data that do not correspond to the label. Unsupervised methods, in turn, often assume smooth latent dynamics and miss genuine discontinuities. We introduce a conceptually simple, computationally efficient latent variable model that infers both (i) the latent variables organizing population activity and (ii) whether their dynamics are continuous or fragmented in time. Fitting reduces to an expectation-maximization (EM) procedure that alternates two operations familiar to systems neuroscience - tuning-curve estimation and label decoding - without requiring external labels. Applied to rodent hippocampal recordings, our method identifies a continuity-fragmentation axis that characterizes population activity across sleep-wake brain states, modulated by cholinergic inputs. For a spatial navigation task, the model reveals distinct population patterns at the same physical position that supervised spatial decoding fails to detect. Moreover, the model enables replay analysis beyond spatial trajectories, and finds prevalent pre-play events associated with immobile and off-maze behaviors and post-task replay of locomotion. By not relying on externally imposed spatial labels, our approach exposes structure that supervised approaches obscure and provides a powerful tool for datasets lacking behavioral tracking.

papers.title: iFLiP: accessible and low-cost lifetime fiber photometry for robust longitudinal and quantitative measurements of neural dynamics.
papers.abstract: Fluorescence lifetime measurements overcome the limitation of widely used intensity-based measurements in quantifying tonic activities and longitudinal changes in neural dynamics. However, while lifetime sensors are rapidly emerging, their applications have been limited by the complexity and expense of required hardware and software. Here, we report a simple, low-cost lifetime fiber photometry system, named iFLiP, that uses entirely off-the-shelf products and can be assembled without specialized expertise. We also develop software that enables turn-key operation. The integrated system can accurately monitor lifetime changes at up to 5000 Hz for days. We demonstrate the utility of iFLiP in monitoring the activity of protein kinase A (PKA) in vitro and in vivo, and uncover striatal subregion- and cell-type-specific PKA dynamics elicited by locomotion in mice. Additionally, multi-day continuous measurements in the basal forebrain reveal previously unappreciated PKA activity associated with sleep/wakefulness. Overall, iFLiP may make lifetime measurements broadly accessible in neuroscience research.

papers.title: Development of Circadian Circuitry Underlying Feeding-Fasting Rhythms in Drosophila Larvae.
papers.abstract: Many organisms do not exhibit strong daily behavioral rhythms early in life. The consolidation of sleep and feeding to specific times of the day does not emerge until later in development. Disruptions to circadian behaviors in early life can lead to dysregulation of both neural development and metabolic homeostasis. However, the circuit mechanisms regulating feeding rhythm development are unknown. Here, we characterize the neural circuitry responsible for driving the development of feeding-fasting rhythms in early 3 rd instar (L3) Drosophila larvae. We find that inactivation of both larval s-LNv circadian pacemaker neurons and SIFamide (SIFa) neurons in the pars intercerebralis disrupts feeding rhythm development. Additionally, our data indicate feeding rhythms likely emerge due to circuit connections forming between s-LNvs and SIFa neurons at the L3 stage. Finally, we show that reductions in signaling between s-LNv and SIFa neurons interfere with normal behavioral rhythm development in L3. Specifically, RNA interference-induced reductions in pigment-dispersing factor ( pdf ) signaling and SIFa signaling disrupt diurnal differences in both feeding and sleep, resulting in a loss of behavioral rhythms. Altogether, our findings identify for the first time the clock and clock output circuitry responsible for feeding rhythm regulation in developing organisms.

papers.title: Housing mice in thermoneutrality causes peripheral tissue-specific changes in the number, identity, and phase of circadian-expressed mRNA transcripts.
papers.abstract: Laboratory mice are typically housed at room temperature (20-25°C), well below their thermoneutral zone (about 30°C), imposing chronic mild cold stress that increases metabolic rate by 30-40%. Because circadian and metabolic physiology are highly temperature-sensitive, we tested whether this housing condition reshapes rhythmic gene expression in tissues central to cardiovascular and metabolic health. We hypothesized that mild cold stress suppresses circadian gene expression in peripheral tissues. We performed RNA sequencing on hearts, livers, and diaphragms collected every 4 hours over 48 hours in constant darkness from male mice to identify transcripts with approximately 24-hour rhythms. Thermoneutral housing reorganized the circadian transcriptome tissue-specifically. Out of ∼13000 filtered transcripts, the proportion of rhythmic transcripts (q<0.05) in the heart nearly quadrupled, from 11% (1410) at room temperature to 42% (5282) at thermoneutrality, while the diaphragm rose modestly (6% to 9%; 792 vs. 1153). The liver's overall proportion was unchanged (36% vs. 37%; 4041 vs. 4150), yet more than 30% of rhythmic transcripts were unique between housing conditions. Almost 80% of rhythmic genes in the heart under thermoneutrality show acrophase near the subjective activity/rest transition. Gene ontology analysis revealed coordinated changes in the temporal organization of metabolic pathways in the heart and liver but less pronounced in the diaphragm. These changes occurred without detectable changes in core clock expression, implicating regulators acting downstream of, or parallel to, the clock itself. Because room temperature housing is standard across biomedical research, our findings show that this overlooked variable can distort the circadian transcriptome of tissues central to cardiovascular and metabolic disease, with implications for how mouse studies model human physiology.

papers.title: Camus: a video-based framework for continuous behavioral monitoring in the mouse home-cage.
papers.abstract: Home-cage activity is a window into the spontaneous behavioral repertoire of mice. These behaviors are organized across the circadian cycle, and disruptions in their duration, frequency, or organization may provide sensitive measures of neurological or psychiatric dysfunction. While continuous monitoring can help track the dynamics of spontaneous behavior, video recording in conventional laboratory cages is limited by compact cage geometry, opaque cage tops, and obstructed views of animals, food, and water. We therefore developed Camus , a Camera for home-cage recordings of Mus musculus mice. Camus integrates off-the-shelf USB cameras with infrared illumination and custom 3D-printed components for access to food and water without obstructed views. The modular design pairs continuous video acquisition with a manually validated computer-vision model to quantify locomotion, feeding, drinking, and nesting-related behavior across multiday recordings. A single desktop computer can record as many as 20 cages in parallel at an incremental cost of approximately $250 per cage, recording more than 99% of expected frames at 640x360-pixel resolution and 30 frames per second. Camus captured circadian structure in locomotion, feeding, and drinking. Camus also captured nest-building and sex-specific differences in nest dynamics. Using Camus with transgenic 5xFAD mice overexpressing amyloid revealed selective, age-progressive deficits in nesting behavior. Camus provides a scalable, open-source platform that combines accessible hardware, automated video monitoring, and machine-learning based analysis for continuous and potentially longitudinal behavioral phenotyping.

papers.title: Assessing non-invasive glymphatic MRI markers following short-term sleep loss.
papers.abstract: The glymphatic system is a sleep-active pathway involved in clearing metabolic waste from the brain. Several non-invasive MRI indices have been proposed as proxies for assessing glymphatic function in vivo . However, it remains unclear whether these indices capture glymphatic dysregulation under short-term sleep loss. Using a large ENIGMA-sleep intervention dataset (n = 429) spanning ten international sites, we examined choroid plexus volume (ChPV), perivascular space volume (PVSV), the free water index (FWI), and the DTI-ALPS index, following habitual sleep (6-8 hours in bed), sleep restriction (3-6 hours in bed), and sleep deprivation (22-40 hours wakefulness). Sleep deprivation was primarily associated with decreased PVSV and ALPS and increased FWI; sleep restriction with the inverse pattern. However, coupling between MRI indices was limited, and models assuming a shared underlying glymphatic system underperformed. Age-related alterations were dissociable from sleep-related alterations and mimicked patterns previously interpreted as glymphatic dysfunction in the literature. Moreover, PVSV increased during the day, whereas ALPS and FWI followed a divergent, anticorrelated trajectory. Our findings suggest that these MRI indices reflect distinct physiological processes; and that sleep loss may influence brain fluid dynamics primarily by modulating inflow resistance through expansion and contraction of the PVS.

papers.title: Autonomic and Cortical Signatures of Sleepiness After Prolonged Sleep Deprivation: Pupillary Reflex, Hippus Oscillations, and Visual Evoked Potentials.
papers.abstract: To define physiologically interpretable visual biomarkers of progressive sleepiness during 48-hour total sleep deprivation and determine whether pupillary and cortical visual measures detect changes not captured by brief behavioral or resting cardiovascular assessments. Twenty-four healthy adults completed one rested baseline assessment and eight supervised deprivation sessions across 48 hours of continuous wakefulness. The protocol included digital pupillometry during the pupillary light reflex (PLR) and Pupillary Sleepiness Test (PST), pattern-reversal and flash visual evoked potentials (VEPs), Stanford Sleepiness Scale (SSS) ratings, selected psychophysiological tasks, and resting blood pressure and heart rate measurements. PLR latency, reaction duration, and time to minimum diameter changed early, indicating slowed reflex timing. With advanced deprivation, DDil1 and DDil2 (pupil diameters at predefined early and late stages of redilation) decreased, identifying them as recovery-phase markers beyond classical PLR indices. The absolute Pupillary Unrest Index (PUI), measuring spontaneous pupillary oscillations (hippus), rose during the first deprivation night and remained elevated; the pupil-size-normalized rPUI followed slightly later, whereas mean pupil diameter was less informative. VEPs added a cortical layer: peak latencies of the pattern-reversal P100 and N135 and flash N3 and P3 components were delayed after prolonged wakefulness. SSS ratings increased progressively, while brief psychophysiological task performance and resting cardiovascular measures remained comparatively stable. Prolonged wakefulness was reflected by a temporally organized visual biomarker profile spanning phasic pupillary reflex timing, dilation-phase recovery, tonic pupillary instability, and late cortical visual-response slowing. These findings support a candidate multimodal, non-invasive framework for objective assessment of progressive sleepiness.

papers.title: Tumbly: An Open-Source Home-Cage Device for Time-Restricted Feeding in Mice.
papers.abstract: Time-restricted feeding (TRF) is a common tool for studying metabolism, circadian rhythms, aging, and neurodegeneration. Here, we describe a new device called Tumbly, an automated device for performing TRF studies in mouse home-cages. Tumbly controls access to rodent diets at user-set times via a programmable servo-driven food hopper. Tumbly is also battery powered and compatible with multiple types of vivarium home-cages, due to a removable faceplate that can be customized to fit different cage dimensions without modification. Finally, Tumbly is open-source and affordable, with all design files available online, allowing researchers to build and customize it. As a validation test, we deployed Tumbly in two labs at separate institutions, one with singly housed mice (n = 6, within-subject) and one with group-housed mice (n = 22, between-group). We measured daily body weight and food intake. In both labs, mice on an 8-hour TRF schedule maintained their body weight and ate similar amounts of food compared to ad libitum feeding. Our quantified error rates were also low, with no device failures over >1000 hours of operation. We conclude that Tumbly provides a reliable, low-cost option for running TRF studies in mice. Time-restricted feeding (TRF) studies are often run by hand, moving food or animals between cages at fixed times to restrict feeding. This approach limits the study cohort size to what experimenters can manage, requires someone to be present to control food at inconvenient hours, and can add stress to the animals from repeated experimenter interventions. Tumbly removes these limitations by automating the TRF procedure. Tumbly is also open-source and can be modified to adapt it to more complex monitoring experiments, such as adding in-cage temperature or humidity sensors. Finally, because Tumbly is affordable, it makes automation of TRF both more accessible to labs with smaller budgets and scalable for researchers that need to run high throughput TRF studies.

papers.title: A Benchmark of Unsupervised Circadian Phase Inference Methods for Bulk Transcriptomic Data.
papers.abstract: Circadian phase can be inferred from gene expression when sample collection times are unavailable, but the available methods have not been systematically compared. We compared ten unsupervised phase inference methods and two clock-gene baselines on 25 datasets with reference times (16 real datasets from five studies and 9 simulations). The primary measure was the aligned circular mean absolute error (MAE), with a permutation test for significance, circular correlations and gene-level reconstruction of rhythmicity, acrophase and amplitude were secondary outcomes. CHIRAL had the lowest mean MAE (1.80 h, 95% confidence interval 1.21-2.97 h from resampling study families). The two clock-gene baselines (2.15 and 2.20 h) were next, followed by TEMPO, CYCLOPS and CYCLOPS 2.0 (2.49-2.80 h), and the confidence intervals of these six overlapped substantially. The other six methods had mean errors of 3.91-4.86 h, compared with 5.08-5.23 h for permuted phases. Accuracy depended on the dataset and on the strength of clock-gene rhythms, and, for several methods, on the random seed and the adjustment for batch or covariates. When the inferred phases were used to analyse gene rhythms in 22 datasets, the four leading methods identified rhythmic genes with a median ROC AUC of 0.64-0.70 and recovered gene acrophases with a median error of 0.18-0.64 h. In two mouse datasets without collection times, agreement with external reference acrophases differed between methods and tissues.

papers.title: Sleep as a vulnerability marker in clinical high-risk populations. a multimodal systematic review.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances are increasingly recognized as clinically significant features of the psychosis risk state, yet no comprehensive synthesis has examined sleep across all assessment modalities in clinical high-risk (CHR) populations. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, five major databases were searched (January 1995-March 2026) for original studies assessing sleep in CHR populations, with CHR status operationalized through validated instruments. From 5218 citations, 26 studies were included. Sleep disturbances affected 59-80% of CHR individuals. Actigraphy predicted positive symptom worsening at 12-month follow-up. Experience sampling identified nocturnal awakenings as predictors of next-day paranoia and derealization, mediated by morning negative affect. Sleep disturbance predicted symptom severity over time, accelerated transition among converters, and was independently associated with suicidal ideation. High-density EEG polysomnography documented reduced prefrontal spindle duration, elevated non-rapid eye movement (NREM) gamma power, and reduced slow wave density - replicated across independent cohorts. A multimodal neuroimaging study identified whole-thalamus-dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) hypoconnectivity as a convergent thalamocortical marker. Sleep disturbances in CHR populations span multiple neurobiologically distinct domains. Polysomnographic markers - spindle parameters and NREM gamma power - represent the most neurophysiologically specific signatures identified. Standardized sleep assessment should be integrated into CHR clinical protocols as both a prognostic tool and a modifiable therapeutic target.

papers.title: EEG-SDL-Net: biomedical EEG signal classification via multi-level supervised Kolmogorov-Arnold networks.
papers.abstract: This paper presents a novel supervised deep learning framework for EEG signal classification based on hierarchical one-dimensional convolutional neural networks with Sobel-based temporal enhancement, channel attention, Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KAN), and multi-level deep supervision. The proposed framework is designed to improve feature representation, robustness to EEG variability, and computational efficiency for Edge AI deployment. The proposed architecture addresses the challenges of EEG signal variability, nonlinear temporal dynamics, and robust feature extraction. The framework integrates a 1D Sobel projection module for local temporal feature enhancement, a channel-wise attention mechanism for adaptive electrode selection, and KAN to capture complex non-linear relationships. Furthermore, a deep supervision strategy is employed to stabilize training and ensure robust gradient flow. Experimental evaluations on the SEED-VIG dataset demonstrate that the proposed model achieves superior classification accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods. Performance benchmarks on edge devices, such as the Raspberry Pi 4, show a real-time inference latency of 15 ms, confirming the framework's suitability for Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) and portable monitoring systems. The complete source code has been made openly available and permanently archived through Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21441822.

papers.title: Circadian phase alignment promotes survival under predictive oxidative stress.
papers.abstract: Circadian clocks are endogenous time-keeping mechanisms that continue to oscillate with a period that approximates 24 h in the absence of cyclic environmental cues. This free-running period (FRP) varies from species to species and can vary within species across latitudinal clines. Because natural environments provide daily cues that reset circadian clocks to exactly 24 h, the importance of the FRP length is unclear. Using the cyanobacterium Synechococcus elongatus we show that the FRP length alters the alignment of a biological process with an environmental reference, known as phase angle of entrainment, across seasonal photoperiods, thereby repositioning stress-response programs relative to the external environment. This phase relationship affects the overall fitness of the organism: strains that position stress-response programs to peak at the time at which the stressor peaks outcompete their early- or late-peaking counterparts. Our results suggest that the FRP length is selected for its ability to adjust the phase angle of entrainment across seasonal photoperiods: the wild-type FRP length was uniquely plastic in its ability to adjust stress-response programs to coincide with the stressor in all photoperiod conditions. Circadian clocks are nearly universal biological timing systems that allow organisms to anticipate daily environmental changes, optimize environmental resources, and avoid environmental threats. We investigated which features of clock function promote survival fitness and which environmental conditions provide selection. A long-standing hypothesis is that the phase relationship between the internal timing mechanism and the external environment is critical for the circadian clock to confer a fitness advantage. However, because this phase relationship is influenced by the circadian period, tests of this hypothesis confound the two features. We experimentally decoupled the free-running period and the environmental phase relationship to show that the phase relationship, rather than the free-running period, confers fitness under environmental conditions that impose a selection.

papers.title: Altered EEG-derived co-fluctuation structure in disorders of consciousness.
papers.abstract: EEG-derived functional connectivity (FC) enables high-temporal-resolution probing of neural mechanisms underlying disorders of consciousness (DOC). Unlike stationary conventional FC, dynamic FC (dFC) captures fast transient neural coupling. Recent fMRI studies introduced a co‑fluctuation framework to track moment‑to‑moment connectivity change, yet whether such co-fluctuation features can quantify consciousness status remains elusive. Here, we adapt this established co-fluctuation paradigm to resting-state EEG to characterize the temporal architectures of EEG-derived FC across varying conscious states. We decomposed the co-fluctuation time series into high-amplitude frames (HAF) and low-amplitude frames (LAF), comparing their dynamics between real brain data and null models. We then analyzed co-fluctuation activities across consciousness levels at both global and local spatial scales, examining spatial variability in these patterns. By integrating HAF and LAF parameters, we evaluated their diagnostic potential for distinguishing DOC states. Results revealed reduced stability of co-fluctuations with loss of consciousness, accompanied by a shift toward random system dynamics. DOC patients exhibited reduced spatial and temporal heterogeneity in co-fluctuation activities compared to healthy controls. Both high- and low-amplitude patterns provided useful metrics for detecting consciousness levels. These findings offer novel insights into the dynamic organization of brain networks in DOC, emphasizing the significance of co-fluctuation dynamics in characterizing brain states and suggesting potential biomarkers for assessing consciousness levels. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s11571-026-10580-7.

papers.title: Functional and Structural Neuroanatomic Correlates of Intraoperative Anesthetic Dose-Adjusted EEG Alpha Power Among Older Surgical Patients.
papers.abstract: Alterations in intraoperative electroencephalography (EEG) alpha power and anesthetic dose-adjusted EEG alpha power (ADA-FP alpha power) have been associated with both preoperative cognitive impairment and postoperative delirium (POD) among older surgical patients, yet the neurologic underpinnings of alterations in these anesthetic brain response patterns are unknown. We conducted a single center prospective observational cohort study (ALADDIN), of older adults undergoing non-cardiac/non-cranial surgery, which included preoperative structural and resting state functional MRI, lumbar punctures to obtain CSF, 32 channel intraoperative EEG recordings, and repeated POD assessments. To account for anesthetic dose, frontoparietal EEG alpha power (ADA-FP alpha power) was adjusted using our established formula: [intraoperative alpha power]/(2.5 - end-tidal MAC fraction). Multivoxel pattern analysis (MVPA) with follow-up seed-to-voxel analyses identified functional connectivity patterns associated with intraoperative ADA-FP alpha power. Voxel-wise regression analysis with threshold free cluster estimation (TFCE) correction was used to evaluate associations between cortical thickness and ADA-FP alpha power. CSF biomarker values were obtained from NULISA proximity extension assays. Delirium incidence and severity was assessed with the 3-Minute Diagnostic Confusion Assessment Method (3D-CAM). Delirium severity area under the curve (AUC) during hospitalization was defined as the sum of all 3D-CAM delirium severity scores within the postoperative hospitalization period (for up to 7 days after surgery). The Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU) was used in cases of non-verbal/intubated patients. ALADDIN enrolled 215 patients, of whom 168 underwent surgery and had high-quality intraoperative EEG data (44.6% female; mean age 70.9 years). MVPA showed that ADA-FP alpha power was associated with altered functional connectivity within the bilateral frontal poles, left superior frontal gyrus and the right superior parietal lobule (p-FWE < 0.05). Seed-to-voxel analyses revealed that higher ADA-FP alpha power was associated with increased connectivity between DMN MVPA regions and DMN, DAN and salience/ventral attention and decreased connectivity with visual regions. Conversely, right superior parietal lobule connectivity shifted towards greater DMN segregation and increased somatosensory/motor coupling (p-FWE < 0.05). Lower ADA-FP alpha power was also associated with lower cortical thickness in left occipitotemporal and superior parietal cortices (TFCE-corrected p < 0.05). ADA-FP alpha power was also lower among participants with (vs those without) postoperative ward/floor delirium (mean difference, 1.33; 95% CI, 0.22 to 2.44; p=0.019), and ADA-FP alpha power was inversely associated with peak delirium severity (spearman's rho = -0.26; 95% CI, -0.40 to -0.11; p <0.001) and delirium severity AUC (spearman's rho = -0.28; 95% CI, -0.42 to -0.13; p < 0.001). These findings suggest a functional and structural neuroanatomic basis for the decreased EEG ADA-FP alpha power values seen among some older surgical patients, which may explain the association between decreased EEG ADA-FP alpha power and increased rates of both preoperative cognitive impairment and postoperative delirium. More specifically, these findings suggest that altered default mode and dorsal attention network connectivity is linked to decreased EEG ADA-FP alpha power and raise the possibility that preoperative/baseline functional connectivity alterations within these networks may play a role in delirium risk.

papers.title: Wearable Technologies to Improve Physical Activity, Sedentary Breaks, Training, Sleep, and Safety: The ECSS-Wearable Technologies Special Interest Group Calls for Interdisciplinary Collaboration.
papers.abstract: Wearable technologies ("wearables") are lightweight sensor-based devices that detect, analyze, and transmit physiological, biomechanical or environmental data, and are increasingly used across physical activity, sedentary behavior, athletic training, safety and sleep research. Applications include for example large-scale physical activity surveillance, ambulatory assessment, and real-time feedback during athletic training. Despite promising use cases such as heart rate variability-informed endurance training or gait retraining via biomechanical feedback, critical challenges remain. These include insufficient data quality, inadequately evaluated and inaccessible algorithms, limited interoperability between systems, difficulties translating sensor data into actionable insights, and insufficient wearable technology literacy among users. The Wearable Technologies Special Interest Group of the European College of Sport Science (ECSS-WT-SIG) identifies the need for interdisciplinary collaboration to address these challenges. Key priorities include developing regulatory frameworks, promoting standardized and open data infrastructure, improving wearable literacy of users, and conducting rigorous intervention studies under real-world conditions. The ECSS-WT-SIG calls on researchers, industry partners, NGOs, and other stakeholders to collectively advance the scientific and practical application of wearables in physical activity, sedentary behavior, training, sleep, and safety research.

papers.title: Rapid Eye Movement Sleep Behavior Disorder as a Prodromal Manifestation of Alpha-Synucleinopathies.
papers.abstract: Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder (RBD) is a parasomnia in which patients physically act out their dreams due to loss of the normal muscle paralysis that occurs during REM sleep. It is now recognized that isolated RBD (iRBD) is strongly associated with future development of α-synuclein-related neurodegenerative diseases, including Parkinson disease (PD), dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), and multiple system atrophy (MSA). It is seen that most patients with polysomnography-confirmed iRBD eventually develop a clinically defined synucleinopathy, often after a long symptom-free interval. This long prodromal phase makes iRBD a unique clinical model for studying the earliest stages of neurodegeneration, before the onset of clear motor or cognitive disability. α-synuclein pathology frequently begins in the lower brainstem and autonomic nervous system, affecting REM sleep regulatory circuits early in the disease process. As pathology spreads, dopaminergic, cholinergic, and cortical systems become involved, leading to the gradual emergence of motor, autonomic, and cognitive symptoms. As a result, many individuals with iRBD exhibit subtle non-motor features such as hyposmia, constipation, orthostatic hypotension, anxiety, and mild cognitive changes years before a formal neurological diagnosis is made. Recent advances have improved the ability to identify patients at the highest risk of near-term phenoconversion. Quantitative measures of REM sleep without atonia, dopamine transporter imaging, autonomic testing, and emerging molecular biomarkers, including α-synuclein seed amplification assays, have shown promise in risk stratification. In addition, cognitive changes may occur earlier than previously recognized, particularly in patients with iRBD who also demonstrate hyposmia or dopaminergic dysfunction. Management of RBD remains largely symptomatic and focuses on injury prevention and sleep stabilization. While clonazepam and melatonin remain first-line therapies, alternative treatments including sodium oxybate, serotonergic agents, cannabinoids, and modulation of the gut-brain axis through probiotic supplementation have also been explored. This narrative review summarizes current knowledge regarding the clinical features, mechanisms, biomarkers, and management of RBD as a prodromal manifestation of α-synucleinopathies, with emphasis on its importance for early diagnosis and future disease-modifying research.

papers.title: Intervention with Exogenous Melatonin Has No Adverse Effects on Cardiometabolic Parameters of Overweight Night Workers without Cardiometabolic Abnormalities.
papers.abstract: Night workers are chronically exposed to circadian disruption and melatonin suppression, conditions associated with an increased risk of cardiometabolic disorders. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover trial was conducted. Participants (n = 27) took 3 mg of fast-release melatonin or placebo orally for 3 months, 1 hour before bedtime, only on days off when they had nocturnal sleep, on an intermittent basis (every other day). Generalized estimating equations (GEEs) were used to analyze the cardiometabolic parameters. Systolic blood pressure showed a significant effect of time ( p = 0.01). Bonferroni-adjusted post-hoc comparisons showed higher values after placebo than at baseline (mean difference: 5.82 mmHg; 95%CI: 2.02-9.62; adjusted p = 0.01), whereas the difference between melatonin and placebo was not statistically significant (adjusted p = 1.00). No statistically significant effects of time were detected for the other cardiometabolic parameters. Melatonin was not associated with significant changes in cardiometabolic parameters compared with placebo in overweight night workers.

papers.title: Cardiac remodeling, autonomic parameters, and clinical factors associated with obstructive sleep apnea: a case-control study.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is associated with substantial cardiovascular morbidity through mechanisms involving intermittent hypoxia, sympathetic activation, oxidative stress, and progressive cardiac remodeling. The present study aimed to comprehensively evaluate clinical characteristics, echocardiographic abnormalities, autonomic function, and independent factors associated with OSA in a case-control population. This observational, case-control study included 108 adults recruited from a tertiary sleep laboratory, 54 patients with OSA and 54 controls selected using frequency matching for age and sex and considered at low risk for OSA based on STOP-Bang screening. Clinical characteristics, cardiovascular risk factors, transthoracic echocardiographic parameters, structural cardiac abnormalities, and 24-hour Holter-derived autonomic indices were compared between groups. Continuous variables were analyzed using the Mann-Whitney U test, categorical variables using Pearson's chi-square or Fisher's exact test, and univariable and multivariable binary logistic regression analyses were performed to identify variables independently associated with OSA. Compared with controls, patients with OSA had significantly higher prevalences of obesity, smoking, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and ischemic heart disease (IHD). Echocardiography demonstrated larger left atrial and right ventricular diameters, higher pulmonary artery systolic pressure (PASP), and increased frequencies of left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH), diastolic dysfunction, and moderate tricuspid regurgitation (TR). Among the Holter-derived autonomic parameters, the root mean square of successive differences between adjacent normal-to-normal intervals (RMSSD) was significantly lower in patients with OSA in the unadjusted comparison. In multivariable linear regression analyses, the association between OSA and RMSSD was attenuated and did not reach statistical significance, while OSA was not independently associated with the standard deviation of normal-to-normal intervals (SDNN). In univariable logistic regression analyses, obesity, smoking, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, ischemic heart disease, left ventricular hypertrophy, and diastolic dysfunction were significantly associated with OSA. After multivariable adjustment, obesity [adjusted odds ratio (OR) 10.86, 95% confidence intervals (CI) 2.99-39.47], smoking (adjusted OR 4.88, 95% CI 1.32-18.14), ischemic heart disease (adjusted OR 19.17, 95% CI 1.65-222.41), and left ventricular hypertrophy (adjusted OR 3.54, 95% CI 1.01-12.40) remained independently associated with OSA. OSA was associated with structural cardiovascular abnormalities and an unadjusted difference in the Holter-derived autonomic parameter RMSSD, whereas neither RMSSD nor SDNN showed a statistically significant independent association with OSA after multivariable adjustment. Obesity, smoking, ischemic heart disease, and left ventricular hypertrophy were independently associated with the presence of OSA, underscoring the close relationship between sleep-disordered breathing and cardiovascular disease. Comprehensive cardiovascular evaluation may improve risk stratification and support earlier identification of patients at increased cardiovascular risk.

papers.title: Real-time wearable detection of respiratory infections in pediatric transplant households.
papers.abstract: Consumer-grade wearables can continuously and longitudinally measure health signals such as heart rate (HR), activity, and sleep. While changes in these signals have been implicated in the early detection of infection (e.g., influenza, SARS-CoV-2) and real-time alerting systems have been developed, evidence from prospective deployment in pediatric transplant households remains limited. Here, we study the application of a resting heart rate (RHR)-based real-time alerting algorithm to detect respiratory virus infection in a cohort of solid organ transplant recipients and their household members (n=146) in a Phase IV clinical trial ( NCT06161454 ). Reliable and efficient alerting for infection events may be particularly relevant for this population, enabling isolation, clinical management, and/or treatment. Of 31 antigen-test outcomes, nearly all (29/31, 93.5%) correspond to either influenza, COVID, or other patient-reported symptoms. We describe RHR, HR, activity, and sleep/circadian rhythm features around clinical alarm events, identifying candidate features for further investigation and algorithm improvement.

papers.title: Time-of-Day Variation in Airway Hyperresponsiveness in Asthma: Potential Circadian Mechanisms and Translational Implications.
papers.abstract: Airway hyperresponsiveness (AHR) is a key physiological feature of asthma and contributes to excessive airway narrowing in response to diverse stimuli. Although asthma-related airway physiology exhibits marked temporal variation, whether AHR itself is independently regulated by the endogenous circadian clock remains unclear. In this narrative review, we summarize current evidence on the definition and temporal phenotype of AHR, with particular emphasis on distinguishing clock-time variation from endogenous circadian regulation and on direct evidence from bronchial provocation studies. We further discuss potential mechanisms linking circadian biology to AHR, including neuroendocrine and autonomic gating, epithelial-immune temporal coupling, airway smooth muscle reactivity, and metabolic and redox regulation. Current evidence supports substantial time dependence of asthma-related airway physiology, whereas direct evidence for an intrinsic circadian rhythm of AHR in humans remains limited with mechanistic insights derived predominantly from animal, ex vivo, and cellular studies. We also review time-dependent treatment strategies, particularly inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) administration, while distinguishing clinically investigated dosing schedules from experimental clock-targeted interventions. Overall, circadian biology provides a framework for understanding temporal variation in AHR and may inform future approaches to phenotyping and treatment timing; however, circadian-based AHR management and clock-targeted therapies remain investigational and require validation in well-controlled human studies.

papers.title: Factors associated with postoperative sleep disturbance in patients undergoing thoracoscopic radical resection for lung cancer: a retrospective cohort study.
papers.abstract: Postoperative sleep disturbance (PSD) is common in patients following surgery, resulting in severe cognitive and mood disturbances, and even increase mortality risk. This study aimed to identify factors associated with PSD in patients undergoing thoracoscopic radical resection for lung cancer. We retrospectively identified sixty-two patients who underwent thoracoscopic radical resection of lung cancer at Tangdu Hospital, a tertiary teaching hospital in Xi'an, China, from June 2023 through October 2024. PSD was defined as a Richards-Campbell Sleep Questionnaire (RCSQ) score <60 on postoperative day 2 (POD2). Preoperative sleep quality was assessed using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI). Pain was measured using the Numeric Rating Scale (NRS) at rest and during coughing on POD1 and POD2. intraoperative fluid volume, and POD2 cough-induced pain, selected a priori based on clinical relevance and prior evidence. Univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed to identify factors independently associated with PSD. Of 62 patients (mean age 67.5 years; 45.2% female), 36 (58.1%) met the RCSQ-defined criteria for PSD on POD2. Three factors were independently associated with PSD: preoperative PSQI score [odds ratio (OR) =1.58, 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.19-2.10, P=0.001], intraoperative fluid volume (OR =1.004 per mL, 95% CI: 1.001-1.007, P=0.02), and POD2 cough-induced pain (OR =2.23 per point, 95% CI: 1.36-3.66, P=0.001). The model demonstrated good calibration (Hosmer-Lemeshow P=0.10) and discrimination (Nagelkerke R2=0.652). Preoperative sleep quality, intraoperative fluid volume, and POD2 cough-induced pain were independently associated with PSD in this cohort. These exploratory findings highlight the importance of closer assessment of potentially high-risk patients, but require validation in larger prospective studies before being translated into definitive preventive strategies.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence-generated and algorithmically personalized music interventions and their effects on brain function, behavior, and health: a critical review.
papers.abstract: This critical review synthesizes empirical studies of algorithmically personalized and artificial-intelligence-generated music interventions reporting neurophysiological, neuroimaging, or objective behavioral outcomes. Literature was identified through structured searches of PubMed, Scopus, Google Scholar, IEEE Xplore, and the ACM Digital Library through 12 August 2026, with CNKI and Wanfang searched on 22 September 2026, supplemented by citation tracking. Twenty-one eligible studies (at least 1,005 participants) were identified. Five things the term artificial intelligence covers in this literature are separated: algorithmic selection from a corpus, rule-based sonification, parametric modulation of pre-existing material, machine-learning generative composition, and closed-loop delivery contingent on the listener's own signal. Only three studies used a machine-learning generative model, so most of the evidence concerns algorithmic personalization of existing material. Studies of closed-loop neural systems reported the most consistent neurophysiological signal, and music-based alpha neurofeedback produced higher normalized alpha power than yoked random feedback. In an open-loop design, personalized EEG-derived music was reported to attenuate anxiety induction where self-selected preferred music and silence did not, with enhanced prefrontal theta oscillations as the associated correlate. Eight studies carried a comparator capable of isolating an algorithmic component from music exposure, and all eight favored the algorithmic condition. These eight address different causal questions, use different designs, and point to no single mechanism, so their results are best read as preliminary and hypothesis-generating. Evidence quality was very low throughout. The median reported sample size was 22, no study blinded participants or measured expectancy, and no specific finding has been independently replicated. GRADE certainty was very low for every outcome domain, covering EEG oscillatory power, sleep architecture, autonomic regulation, epileptiform activity, and cognitive, behavioral and affective outcomes. Neurophysiological change is reported more often than behavioral change, and behavioral change more often than clinical benefit. The evidence supports continued investigation and does not support clinical deployment. Eight reporting and design requirements for future trials are proposed.

papers.title: Longitudinal Pain Profiles and Their Clinical and Genetic Correlates in 624,996 U.S. Veterans.
papers.abstract: Pain varies in its intensity and course, yet much of our understanding of pain is based on cross-sectional assessments or longitudinal studies of selected clinical populations. Routinely collected electronic health record data may enable characterization of longitudinal pain patterns at scale. To identify longitudinal pain profiles among U.S. Veterans and characterize their clinical and polygenic correlates. Cohort study using electronic health record and genomic data from the Million Veteran Program, with up to 16 years of pain assessments collected between 2000 to 2025. U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs health care system. Million Veteran Program participants assigned to African-like, Admixed American-like, East Asian-like, European-like, or South Asian-like genetically inferred ancestry groups who have at least three years of outpatient numeric rating scale pain records. Outpatient pain ratings and polygenic scores for psychiatric, sleep, and substance use traits. Pain profiles were identified using Gaussian finite mixture modeling of pain intensity, directional change, and within-person variability. Profiles were characterized by pain, psychiatric and substance use diagnoses, opioid exposure, body mass index, and polygenic scores. Among 624,996 participants (Mean [SD] age at first pain rating=53.4 [13.5] years; 568,833 [91.0%] male), 51,731,567 outpatient pain ratings were analyzed. Three profiles were identified: stable no pain, stable mild pain, and mild-to-moderate increasing pain. Compared with the stable no pain profile, the increasing pain profile had higher odds of chronic pain (OR=21.14 [95% CI: 18.96-23.57]), opioid use disorder (OR=9.32 [95% CI: 8.31-10.45]), opioid exposure (OR=8.61 [95% CI: 8.41-8.83]), major depressive disorder (OR=3.77 [95% CI: 3.67-3.87]), and posttraumatic stress disorder (OR=3.72 [95% CI: 3.61-3.84]). Associations were attenuated but remained after adjustment for mean pain severity. Polygenic scores for depression, insomnia, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, and tobacco use disorder were the most consistent predictors of increasing pain across the three largest genetically inferred ancestry groups. Longitudinal modeling of routinely collected pain scores identified pain profiles associated with clinical burden and polygenic liability. These profiles captured clinically meaningful information beyond mean pain severity alone, highlighting the value of longitudinal pain phenotyping in electronic health record data. papers.title: Postoperative changes in primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis following adenoidectomy or adenotonsillectomy in children with adenotonsillar hypertrophy and sleep-disordered breathing: A prospective cohort study.

The complementary mean reduction was 2.74 nights/week (95% CI, 2.41-3.08). Median mESS score decreased from 4 (IQR, 3-5) to 2 (IQR, 0-3; P < 0.001). papers.title: Circadian blood pressure adaptation and arterial stiffness in pregnancy: An exploratory study.

papers.abstract: BackgroundPostoperative delirium is a common perioperative complication. Early randomised trials suggested that non-invasive brain stimulation may reduce postoperative delirium, whereas the recent MODEST trial found no preventive benefit. We synthesised the randomised evidence for perioperative non-invasive brain stimulation. MethodsWe searched eight bibliographic databases and ClinicalTrials.gov from inception to 30 September 2026 for randomised controlled trials of perioperative non-invasive brain stimulation in adults undergoing surgery. The primary outcome was postoperative delirium. Random-effects meta-analyses estimated risk ratios (RRs), mean differences, or standardised mean differences. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2 and certainty of evidence using GRADE. ResultsNine trials contributed data from 1451 participants. Postoperative delirium occurred in 72 of 750 participants receiving active stimulation and 166 of 701 controls (RR 0.41, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.31-0.56; I2=24.7%; moderate-certainty evidence). Estimates also favoured stimulation for hypoactive and hyperactive delirium, but not clearly for mixed delirium. Pain, anxiety, and sleep outcomes favoured stimulation but were highly heterogeneous and supported by very-low-certainty evidence. Length of hospital stay was not reduced. Adverse events could not be pooled because reporting was incomplete and inconsistent. ConclusionsPerioperative non-invasive brain stimulation may reduce postoperative delirium, but the evidence does not establish a class effect or support routine clinical use. Geographical concentration, methodological concerns, heterogeneous stimulation protocols, and discordance with the MODEST trial warrant independent multicentre sham-controlled trials. papers.title: Efficacy and safety of commercial Chinese polyherbal preparations combined with biomedicine for elderly patients with primary insomnia: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
papers.abstract: The prevalence of primary insomnia among the elderly is steadily increasing; however, robust evidence supporting the efficacy and safety of combining commercial Chinese polyherbal preparations (CCPPs) with biomedicine therapy remains insufficient. This study aimed to systematically evaluate the efficacy and safety of CCPPs combined with biomedicine versus biomedicine therapy for primary insomnia in elderly patients, and to assess the certainty of the evidence via the GRADE framework and P-curve analysis. Seven biomedical databases were searched (before November 2025) for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving elderly patients with primary insomnia. Risk of bias was assessed using Cochrane RoB 2 by two researchers independently. Meta-analysis was performed using R software. Outcomes included Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), total clinical effectiveness rate, Sleep Dysfunction Rating Scale (SDRS), and adverse events. Robustness was evaluated via sensitivity, subgroup, and P-curve analyses. Meta-analysis suggested that combined therapy was associated with a lower PSQI score (MD = -2.09, 95% CI -2.62 to -1.57) and higher total clinical effectiveness rate (RR = 1.21, 95% CI 1.15-1.27) relative to monotherapy. The combination group also showed a lower risk of adverse events (RR = 0.47, 95% CI 0.36-0.61). However, P-curve analysis revealed notable discrepancies across outcomes: PSQI exhibited sufficient evidential value (Power = 99%), whereas the total clinical effectiveness rate lacked adequate evidential value (Power = 9%), implying potential publication bias. Subgroup analyses showed that heterogeneity decreased within the subgroup of patients with disease duration <1 year, although the between-subgroup difference did not reach statistical significance. The certainty of evidence was rated as "Moderate" for adverse events but "Low" to "Very Low" for efficacy outcomes. In elderly patients with primary insomnia, combined treatment of CCPPs and biomedicine may help improve sleep quality and may reduce adverse events reported in clinical trials. However, due to methodological limitations, high heterogeneity and potential publication bias among the included trials, the certainty of the available evidence remains limited. Given insufficient evidential value, the reliability of the total clinical effectiveness rate is questionable, and clinicians should place greater emphasis on outcomes assessed using validated scales such as the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI). Further large-scale, multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are needed to further verify these preliminary findings. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251186213, identifier: CRD420251186213.

papers.title: Symptom and Quality-Of-Life Trajectories After High-Intensity Focused Ultrasound in Patients with Advanced Cancer: Exploratory Associations with Overall Survival in a Prospective Pilot Study.
papers.abstract: Patients with advanced cancer frequently experience substantial symptom burden and impaired quality of life (QoL). This study aimed to characterize longitudinal trajectories of patient-reported symptoms and QoL after high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) and to explore their associations with subsequent overall survival (OS). This exploratory prospective longitudinal pilot cohort study enrolled 54 patients with malignant solid tumors who underwent HIFU. Patient-reported symptoms and QoL were assessed using a study-specific 14-item symptom checklist and the EORTC QLQ-C30 at five post-HIFU time points: day 1 (D1), week 1, month 1 (M1), month 2, and month 3. Longitudinal outcomes were summarized descriptively. Exploratory associations with OS were examined using Kaplan-Meier analyses and univariable Cox proportional hazards models. At D1, the most prevalent symptoms were sleep disturbance (55.56%), back pain (44.44%), dry mouth (35.19%), hiccup (29.63%), and dysphoria (25.93%). The mean severity scores of the five most severe symptoms at D1 reached their lowest observed values at M1, while QoL reached its highest observed mean score at M1 (77.41). Median OS was 298 days (95% CI, 209 days to not reached). In exploratory univariable Cox analyses, back pain at D1 (HR = 2.25, 95% CI 1.13-4.47; p = 0.021) and hiccup at D1 (HR = 2.12, 95% CI 1.06-4.24; p = 0.034) were associated with a higher hazard of death. Each 10-point increase in global health status/QoL at D1 was associated with a lower hazard of death (HR = 0.81, 95% CI 0.68-0.98; p = 0.024). In this exploratory pilot cohort, several patient-reported symptoms and QoL measures showed their most favorable observed values at approximately one month after HIFU. Back pain, hiccup, and QoL showed exploratory associations with OS. These preliminary findings may inform post-HIFU symptom and QoL assessment and warrant validation in larger prospective studies.

papers.title: Pain Management in Orthopedic Surgery: A Procedure-Specific Orthopedic-Anesthesia Approach to Perioperative Analgesia.
papers.abstract: Introduction: Post-operative pain in orthopedic surgery is clinically important because inadequate analgesia can impair mobilization, sleep, physiotherapy and discharge, while excessive analgesia can cause sedation, motor weakness, drug toxicity and unnecessary opioid exposure. This narrative review uses a structured literature search of PubMed/MEDLINE and targeted review of recent systematic reviews, randomized trials, consensus statements and procedure-specific recommendations, with emphasis on publications available through September 2026. Evidence is synthesized qualitatively according to procedure, analgesic strategy, functional outcomes, and limitations of the underlying evidence. Present evidence supports multimodal analgesia, but does not support a universal regimen or routine addition of every available intervention. Regional techniques can improve early analgesia, although benefits vary by procedure and may be offset by motor block, rebound pain, or limitations in post-operative examination. A non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) provide opioid-sparing analgesia, but the relationship between NSAID exposure and fracture healing remains uncertain and appears to depend on drug, dose, duration, fracture type, and patient factors. Opioids remain appropriate as rescue therapy when clinically indicated. Persistent post-surgical pain is influenced by pre-operative and biopsychosocial factors and acute analgesia has not been shown consistently to prevent it. The practical framework proposed here therefore links the operation, patient risk profile, analgesic options, and rehabilitation task, with unexpected severe pain treated as a trigger for clinical reassessment rather than automatic escalation.

papers.title: Circadian Rhythm-Associated Diagnostic Biomarkers Reveal Immune Dysregulation and Molecular Subtypes in Recurrent Pregnancy Loss.
papers.abstract: Recurrent pregnancy loss (RPL) is a clinically complex reproductive disorder involving impaired maternal-fetal communication and immune imbalance. Circadian rhythm disturbance has recently attracted attention in reproductive failure, but its diagnostic relevance and possible connection with immune dysregulation in RPL remain insufficiently defined. GSE165004 was used as the discovery cohort, and GSE26787 was used as an independent small cohort for preliminary evaluation. Circadian rhythm-associated genes were collected from GeneCards. Differential expression analysis, weighted gene co-expression network analysis, and ssGSEA-based circadian rhythm scoring were integrated to identify RPL-associated circadian transcriptional alterations. Candidate genes were further evaluated by protein-protein interaction analysis, functional enrichment, receiver operating characteristic curve analysis, nomogram construction, immune infiltration assessment, molecular subtype identification, and ceRNA regulatory network prediction. RPL samples showed a significantly lower circadian rhythm-associated gene score than control samples, indicating reduced circadian-associated transcriptional activity. Three genes, GJA1, UCP2, and GSN, were identified as circadian rhythm-associated candidate diagnostic biomarkers for RPL. In the discovery cohort, the AUC values of GJA1, UCP2, and GSN were 0.80, 0.77, and 0.81, respectively. Their diagnostic performance was further evaluated in an independent small cohort, where the AUC values were 0.72, 0.80, and 0.92, respectively. GSN showed a significant expression difference between RPL and control samples in the independent cohort, whereas GJA1 and UCP2 did not reach statistical significance. Immune infiltration analysis revealed changes in fibroblast, neutrophil, macrophage, Treg, T helper cell, and interferon-related signatures. Consensus clustering based on the three biomarkers classified RPL samples into two molecular subtypes with different immune-stromal characteristics, coagulation-related activity, and metabolic features. The ceRNA network contained 3 diagnostic mRNAs, 43 predicted miRNAs, and 61 upstream lncRNAs. GJA1, UCP2, and GSN may represent circadian rhythm-associated candidate biomarkers for RPL. Their expression patterns may reflect circadian-immune dysregulation and molecular heterogeneity. These findings provide a circadian rhythm-based perspective for understanding RPL pathogenesis and nominate candidate molecules for future diagnostic and mechanistic validation.

papers.title: A qualitative exploration of COPD lived experience, giving insight into symptom profile determinants and experiences of medical and non-medical interventions.
papers.abstract: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is characterised by a substantial symptom burden, including reduced physical activity, impaired sleep, diminished quality of life, and psychological distress. Despite established treatments, many individuals continue to experience persistent symptoms and functional limitations. This study aimed to explore symptom burden and how individuals manage COPD in daily life. Fifteen UK-based adults with a confirmed diagnosis of COPD (mean age 70 years, n = 10 females) participated in semi-structured interviews. Participants were recruited through clinical databases, research registries, and community support networks. Interviews were transcribed verbatim and analysed using inductive reflexive thematic analysis supported by NVivo. Three themes were identified: (1) Interconnected symptom experiences, (2) Navigating treatment uncertainty and burden, and (3) Becoming an active manager of COPD. Breathlessness was described as the most debilitating symptom, closely interconnected with reduced functional capacity, and restricted social participation. Participants reported challenges with medication, including frequent treatment changes and limited perceived effectiveness. Self-management was central to daily life, with individuals employing pacing strategies, assistive devices, and self-directed learning. COPD is experienced as a complexcondition shaped by interconnected symptoms and self-management demands. These findings highlight a need for responsive, patient-centred approaches to COPD care.

papers.title: Gut microbiome depletion aggravates glial-mediated Alzheimer's disease pathology through inflammatory, metabolic, and proteostatic dysregulation.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by chronic neuroinflammation, metabolic dysfunction, and impaired proteostasis. Emerging evidence suggests that the gut microbiome influences brain function through the gut-brain axis; however, the mechanisms by which this communication affects AD pathology remain poorly understood. In this study, we used humanized Drosophila AD models expressing human AD-related transgenes in glial cells to investigate how glial AD pathology influences the gut microbiome and how microbiome depletion affects behavior and disease progression. Our findings revealed significant alterations in the abundance of several gut microbial taxa, including Lactobacillus, Acetobacter, Enterococcus, Enterobacter, Pseudomonas, Leuconostoc, Providencia, and Gluconobacter, suggesting a potential interaction between the gut microbiome and AD progression. To further define the role of the gut microbiome in AD progression, we treated Drosophila with antibiotics to achieve substantial microbiome depletion (SMD) and evaluated the resulting behavioral, physiological, and molecular changes. Compared with conventional controls, flies with SMD exhibited enhanced inflammatory signaling and cell death, impaired autophagy, lipid dysregulation, and increased accumulation of amyloid β-42 (aβ42) and phospho-tau (pTau), with the extent of these changes varying among the different humanized AD models. These molecular alterations further exacerbated sleepcircadian disruption, altered locomotor performance, and worsened learning and memory deficits. Furthermore, we demonstrated a link between enhanced neuroinflammation and the accumulation of aβ42, pTau, and amyloid precursor protein (APP) proteins. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that gut microbiome depletion aggravates glial-mediated AD pathology through the coordinated disruption of inflammatory, metabolic, and proteostatic pathways, ultimately leading to behavioral dysfunction. These results identify the gut microbiome as a critical regulator of glial homeostasis and provide new insights into its contribution to the progression of neurodegenerative disorders.

papers.title: Associations Between Psychological Factors, Routine Hematological and Biochemical Indicators, and Non-Suicidal Self-Injury Among University Students: An Exploratory Cross-Sectional Study.
papers.abstract: Non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) is a major mental health concern among university students. Although psychological risk factors for NSSI have been extensively studied, the potential contribution of routinely available hematological and biochemical indicators remains unclear. This study examined their associations with NSSI and their incremental value beyond psychological factors. This cross-sectional study included 1,661 university students who completed campus psychological screening and routine health examinations. NSSI status was defined as an NSSI total score greater than zero. Psychological variables included depressive symptoms, anxiety symptoms, sleep problems, impulsivity, attentional control, cognitive emotion regulation strategies, and problematic internet use. Associations between routine indicators and NSSI severity were examined using Spearman correlations, while logistic regression models evaluated associations with NSSI status after adjustment for demographic and psychological factors. Five-fold cross-validation was used to compare predictive performance across demographic, routine indicator, psychological, and combined models. Among the 1,661 participants, 244 (14.69%) were classified as having NSSI. Several routine indicators, including AST, ALT, red blood cell count, uric acid, hemoglobin, and hematocrit, showed weak correlations with NSSI total scores after FDR correction. However, no routine hematological or biochemical indicator remained significant after false discovery rate (FDR) correction in either adjusted logistic regression model. The psychological model showed substantially better predictive performance than demographic or routine indicator models, and adding routine indicators did not improve prediction (AUC: 0.796 vs. 0.787). Routine hematological and biochemical indicators showed weak associations with NSSI severity but provided limited incremental value beyond psychological factors for identifying NSSI among university students. Psychological assessment remains an important component of NSSI screening, whereas routine laboratory data did not show additional incremental value in this sample.

papers.title: EEG responses to monosodium glutamate concentration and individual umami sensitivity in healthy adults.
papers.abstract: Taste perception depends on stimulus intensity and individual sensitivity, but how these factors shape cortical responses to monosodium glutamate (MSG) is unclear. We combined psychophysics and 64-channel EEG in 38 healthy adults grouped by MSG detection threshold. Increasing MSG concentration reduced fronto-central P200 and posterior N200 amplitudes (FDR-corrected p < .001; partial η2 = 0.30-0.50), and evoked beta power was highest at the lowest concentration. Exploratory source analyses showed weaker right orbitofrontal-dorsolateral prefrontal beta-band (14-30 Hz) connectivity at higher concentrations. The ERP effects were robust to alternative preprocessing. No group effect survived correction, and sensitivity could not be decoded above chance. Lower detection thresholds were associated with larger posterior late positive potentials (exploratory). EEG captures robust neural responses to MSG concentration and may complement sensory panels, whereas neural markers of individual sensitivity require larger samples.

papers.title: Cross-species multi-omics integration reveals lung alterations in acute kidney injury across mouse, pig, and human airway organoid models.
papers.abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is frequently associated with the development of distant acute lung injury (ALI); however, its broader clinical impact and the underlying temporal molecular mechanisms remain incompletely characterized. We used aggregate deidentified Epic Cosmos data to describe all-cause mortality and hospital length of stay (LOS) in an AKI cohort (13,815,092 patients; 2016-2025) and a subgroup with subsequent lung injury (AKI-lung). Mechanistically, we integrated matched RNA-seq and proteomics from a hyper-acute pig model (4 h reperfusion), an established mouse model (24 h reperfusion), and primary lung organoids exposed to mtDAMP-conditioned media, using MOFA+, PROGENy, decoupleR/CollecTRI, and DIABLO. Candidates were validated in primary human donor lungs obtained from LifeLink, separated into Control (< 1.3 mg/dL, n = 5) and AKI (≥ 1.3 mg/dL, n = 5) groups based on the highest blood creatinine level measured in hospital. The AKI-lung subgroup had higher observed mortality than the overall AKI cohort (36.67% vs. 25.45%, p < 0.001). Mean hospital LOS was 11.3 versus 6.9 days in the reported AKI-lung and AKI alone queries, respectively (unadjusted p < 0.001). Multi-omics analyses cross-species indicated a temporal shift in proteogenomic coupling. In the hyper-acute pig model, we observed a largely post-translational response, including ciliary breakdown and metabolic changes. The established mouse model showed a coordinated transcriptional inflammatory response (r = 0.316), characterized by PI3K/Akt pathway activation and downregulation of vascular and immune regulators (Aplnr, Cd74). Human lung organoids exhibited transcriptional downregulation of tissue remodeling genes and persistent ATF6/ATF4-associated ER stress, consistent with a reparative phase under proteostatic strain. Unsupervised MOFA+ revealed conserved cross-species axes (Factors 6 and 7) linked to vascular repair and hemostasis. Upstream regulon analysis identified the endothelial integrity regulators, including FOXF1. Most importantly, targeted validation in primary human donor lungs confirmed a statistically significant, selective down-regulation of the core circadian regulator circadian locomotor output cycles kaput (CLOCK) transcript (p < 0.05). Aggregate clinical findings suggest an association between lung injury following AKI and worse outcome. Kidney-Lung crosstalk initiates as hyper-acute post-translational microvascular breakdown in swine and rapidly transitions into localized uncoupling of cell-autonomous pulmonary circadian machinery (CLOCK) in clinical human AKI, offering human-validated targets to intercept distant organ failure.

papers.title: Adverse childhood experiences, lifestyle-related risks, and suicidal ideation and suicide attempts among Chinese college students: joint associations and exploratory network analysis.
papers.abstract: Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) are established correlates of suicidality, but their joint associations with cumulative lifestyle-related risks during emerging adulthood and the conditional connections among specific indicators remain insufficiently characterized. A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 18,723 college students selected through multistage cluster sampling from six colleges in Shaanxi Province, China. Thirteen ACE domains were assessed using the Adverse Childhood Experiences International Questionnaire. A cumulative lifestyle-related risk score included smoking, drinking, inadequate physical activity, unhealthy body mass index, and unhealthy diet. Suicidal ideation (SI) and suicide attempt (SA) during the past 12 months were self-reported. Modified Poisson regression was used to estimate adjusted prevalence ratios (aPRs). Departure from additivity on the prevalence-ratio scale was evaluated using the relative excess risk due to interaction (RERI) and attributable proportion (AP). Exploratory network models were used to characterize conditional associations and cross-community connectivity. The prevalence of SI and SA was 3.3 and 1.9% during the past 12 months, respectively. Greater ACE exposure and higher cumulative lifestyle-related risk score were associated with a higher prevalence of both outcomes. Compared with participants reporting 0-3 ACEs and 0-1 lifestyle-related risk factors, those reporting ≥4 ACEs and ≥2 lifestyle-related risks had the highest adjusted prevalence ratios of SI (aPR, 8.37; 95% CI, 5.64-11.10) and SA (aPR, 10.30; 95% CI, 5.76-14.85). Positive departure from additivity was observed for SI (RERI, 3.35; 95% CI, 1.03-5.97; AP, 0.40; 95% CI, 0.13-0.62) and SA (RERI, 5.18; 95% CI, 1.92-9.78; AP, 0.50; 95% CI, 0.19-0.75). In the exploratory networks, poor sleep showed high cross-community connectivity, while emotional abuse, bullying, inadequate physical activity, and drinking also showed prominent bridge expected influence. Greater ACE exposure and cumulative lifestyle-related risks were separately and jointly associated with a higher prevalence of SI and SA. Participants reporting both ≥ 4 ACEs and ≥2 lifestyle-related risk profiles had the highest prevalence for SI and SA with evidence of additive interactions. The network results describe cross-sectional conditional associations and should be regarded as hypothesis-generating rather than as evidence of causal or mediating pathways.
